cards.title: Oxidation states name the agents

walkthrough.question:
Hypochlorite ions react with sulfur dioxide in water:
ClO−(aq) + SO2(g) + H2O(l) → Cl−(aq) + SO4 2−(aq) + 2H+(aq)
Which pair gives the oxidizing agent first, then the reducing agent?
A. ClO− and H2O
B. SO2 and SO4 2−
C. SO2 and ClO−
D. ClO− and SO2
walkthrough.key_idea: The oxidizing agent contains the atom reduced; the reducing agent contains the atom oxidized.
walkthrough.question_type: Redox: identify oxidizing and reducing agents
walkthrough.careful: An agent is a reactant species, never a product.
procedure: Assign an oxidation state to each atom on both sides.
Find the atom whose oxidation state falls: it is reduced.
Find the atom whose oxidation state rises: it is oxidized.
Name the reactant species containing each of those atoms.
Reactant holding the reduced atom is the oxidizing agent.
Reactant holding the oxidized atom is the reducing agent.
tricks: Cross out any option naming a product: agents are always reactants.
Water often only balances the equation; fails if its H or O changes state.
if_lost: Which atoms change oxidation state from left to right?
What is the oxidation state of Cl in ClO−?
Does a species containing a reduced atom gain or lose electrons?

1_context.short: Naming agents needs oxidation states, not just spotting oxygen.
1_context.why: Oxygen appears in several species here, so oxygen gain or loss is hard to read. Oxidation states work on every redox equation.
1_context.avoid: Judging by oxygen alone when three reactants contain or supply it.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.1: identify oxidized and reduced species and the oxidizing and reducing agents.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books practise definitions on simple metal reactions. This item uses an oxoanion with water present, so states must be assigned.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only ClO− oxidizing with SO2 reducing earns the mark.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The agent is named after what it does to the other species, so it undergoes the opposite change itself.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Reversing the two agents, reported in 07M.2.HL.TZ0.3 and 13M.2.HL.TZ1.4.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The row must be right in both columns: C holds the correct species in reversed roles and scores nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D names the reactant holding each changing atom. C swaps the roles; B names a product.

3_novel_application.short: Rare hypochlorite hides a simple Cl +1 to −1 change.
3_novel_application.why: Only two atoms change state. Everything else is bookkeeping that balances the equation.
3_novel_application.avoid: Trying to balance half-equations because the species look unfamiliar.
3_novel_application.disguise: Hypochlorite is rarely met, and three reactants suggest a complicated change.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ignore names. Mark only atoms whose state changes, then read off the two reactants holding them.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: choose the row with both roles right.
4_command_terms.why: Each row tests both roles at once, so one correct half gains nothing.
4_command_terms.avoid: Stopping once you have found the oxidizing agent.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the row with the oxidizing agent and reducing agent in the correct columns.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Assign states to Cl and S only, then choose.
5_time_efficiency.why: H stays +1 and O stays −2 in every species, so checking them adds no information.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing out and balancing two half-equations for a one-mark item.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip half-equations and electron counts; two oxidation states settle this.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet help: oxidation state rules must be known.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 19 lists reduction potentials, but ClO− is absent and oxidation state rules are not given.
6_data_booklet.pattern: No table applies; use the rules directly.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: O is usually −2, H usually +1, and states sum to the species' charge.

7_elimination.short: B names a product; water in A does not change.
7_elimination.why: An agent must be present before the reaction to act on another species, and a species with unchanged states is not an agent.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking B because sulfur visibly changes in it.

definitely_wrong.rule: SO4 2− is a product, and agents are reactants.
H and O in water keep their states, so water is not the reducing agent.

walkthrough.answer: D. ClO− is the oxidizing agent (Cl +1 to −1); SO2 is the reducing agent (S +4 to +6).

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.1: deduce oxidation states; identify species oxidized and reduced and the two agents.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stress electron definitions; exams test unfamiliar equations where states must be deduced, including hydrogen as oxidizing agent in a metal hydride.

trigger_phrases: species containing the atom reduced is the oxidizing agent
species containing the atom oxidized is the reducing agent
trap_boundaries: The species must be named: reports record atoms or half-equations given instead (11M.2.HL.TZ2.7, 08M.2.SL.TZ0.8).
Write states with the sign first, +3 not 3+ (12N.2.HL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Knowing the definition is not enough: reports show candidates who define oxidation correctly but cannot name the species or agent (04N.2.HL.TZ0.9, 08N.2.SL.TZ0.5).

disguises: Hydrogen acting as an oxidizing agent when it forms NaH.
Oxoanions and water present in the same equation.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask what changed state first; only then attach the word agent to the reactant holding it.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ is all or nothing; written items often need both agents for the mark, so naming only one risks it.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not assign states to atoms that plainly stay unchanged, such as H in water.

6_data_booklet.hack: Oxidation state rules are NOT in the booklet. Section 19 helps rank agents only when E° values are being compared.

rules: A product cannot be the agent.
A species with no change of state is not an agent.

evidence.note: Worked question; answer D.
Hydrogen as oxidizing agent; answer B, about 65% correct.
Assigning a sulfur oxidation state; answer C, 89% correct.
Agents often missed or given in reverse order.
Named atoms as agents, or reversed the correct answers.
Signs written after the number for oxidation states.
Knew oxidation is electron loss but named bromine, not bromide, as the species oxidized.
Could define oxidation yet not identify the strongest oxidizing agent.

cards.difficulty_signal: Easy on a single state (89%) but harder on roles (about 65%). 'Oxidation numbers', 'reducing agent' and 'oxidizing agent' are all frequent error signals.

cards.title: Multi-step redox: chain the mole ratios

walkthrough.question:
Dissolved oxygen in a 200 cm3 river water sample is measured through three reactions:
Step 1: 2Mn2+(aq) + 4OH−(aq) + O2(aq) → 2MnO2(s) + 2H2O(l)
Step 2: MnO2(s) + 2I−(aq) + 4H+(aq) → Mn2+(aq) + I2(aq) + 2H2O(l)
Step 3: 2S2O3 2−(aq) + I2(aq) → S4O6 2−(aq) + 2I−(aq)
(a) Name the species reduced in step 1, with a reason. [1]
(b) Step 3 forms 4.8 × 10−3 mol of I−. Find the amount of O2 in the sample. [1]
(c) Find the oxygen concentration in g dm−3. [1]
walkthrough.key_idea: O2 is reduced; each O2 leads through the steps to four I−.
walkthrough.question_type: Multi-step redox: reduced species and mole chain
walkthrough.careful: Link every step by its ratio; then convert cm3 to dm3.
procedure: Compare oxidation states of each changing atom in the step.
Name the species whose state falls, and give the reason.
Write each step's mole ratio from its coefficients.
Chain the ratios from the known amount to the target.
Convert amount to mass using the molar mass.
Divide mass by the volume in dm3.
tricks: Scale everything to one O2: 1 O2 → 2 MnO2 → 2 I2 → 4 I−.
Check the unit asked: g dm−3 needs the molar mass as well as volume.
if_lost: Which atom's oxidation state falls in step 1?
How many moles of I2 form from one mole of MnO2?
How many moles of I− form from one mole of I2?
What is 200 cm3 in dm3?

1_context.short: A titration chain joins redox identification with mole ratios.
1_context.why: Each product feeds the next step, so the ratio between first and last species comes from multiplying the links.
1_context.avoid: Using a single step's ratio as the whole chain.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.1: identify the species oxidized and reduced in a chemical reaction.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach redox and stoichiometry separately. This question joins them across three equations with no overall ratio given.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Part (a) needs O2 plus a reason; (c) needs grams.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The species alone does not justify reduction: the mark rests on electron gain or falling oxidation state.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Stopping at mol dm−3 in (c), reported in 24N.2.HL.TZ0.7.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Answers without a reason miss (a). The fallback 2.0 × 10−3 mol earns the mark in (c) with 0.32 g dm−3.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit in (c) multiplies by 32.00 and divides by volume; mol dm−3 answers miss the unit requested.

3_novel_application.short: River-water context hides a plain ratio chain.
3_novel_application.why: The chemistry of Mn and I need not be known: only the printed coefficients matter.
3_novel_application.avoid: Worrying about what the Winkler Method is.
3_novel_application.disguise: An environmental analysis with unfamiliar manganese and thiosulfate species looks like new chemistry.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Find the species shared by consecutive steps; they are the links. Then only coefficients matter.

4_command_terms.short: Identify, determine, calculate: one short mark each.
4_command_terms.why: Each part is worth one mark, so reasoning stays short but the reason in (a) cannot be dropped.
4_command_terms.avoid: Omitting the reason because (a) carries only one mark.
4_command_terms.demands: Name the species with a reason; find the amount of O2; convert it to a mass concentration.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per part; correct final value earns it. The stated fallback amount keeps (c) open if (b) fails.

5_time_efficiency.short: Divide by four, times 32.00, divide by 0.200.
5_time_efficiency.why: The whole calculation is three operations once the four-to-one link is known.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating moles of every intermediate separately and risking a slip.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip intermediates such as moles of thiosulfate; they are not needed here.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 1 gives n = m/M; the chain is your job.
6_data_booklet.why: The booklet gives the amount relation, but deducing mole links and oxidation states comes from the equations and rules.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking in section 19 for these reactions.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Rearrange n = m/M from section 1 to get mass.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Oxidation state rules and the chain method are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: O2 amount must be smaller than I− amount.
7_elimination.why: One O2 produces several iodide ions overall, so a larger O2 amount shows an inverted ratio.
7_elimination.avoid: Multiplying by four instead of dividing.

definitely_wrong.rule: Mn goes from +2 to +4, a rise, so it is oxidized.

definitely_wrong.target: An O2 amount larger than 4.8 × 10−3 mol
definitely_wrong.rule: Four I− form per O2, so O2 must be less.

definitely_wrong.target: A final answer in mol dm−3
definitely_wrong.rule: The unit requested is g dm−3.

walkthrough.answer: (a) O2: it gains electrons / its oxidation state falls from 0 to −2. (b) 4.8 × 10−3 ÷ 4 = 1.2 × 10−3 mol. (c) 1.2 × 10−3 × 32.00 ÷ 0.200 = 0.19 g dm−3.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.1 applied to a sequence of redox equations.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give one titration equation; exams chain several and ask for the overall ratio.

trap_boundaries: A fallback value in a later part still earns the mark with its own answer.
Report: some used 2 instead of 4 for the iodide ratio (14M.3.SL.TZ1.16).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: About half could use the coefficients for a quarter ratio; many then stopped at mol dm−3 instead of g dm−3.

disguises: Winkler Method for dissolved oxygen.
Any sequence of equations sharing an intermediate.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Scale all steps to one mole of the target species and read off the last ratio.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per part here; the reason is part of the mark in (a).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not balance or rewrite the equations given.

6_data_booklet.hack: n = m/M is in section 1. Mole chains and oxidation state rules are NOT in the booklet.

rules: A species whose state rises is not reduced.
The start of a chain producing more product per mole has the smaller amount.

evidence.note: Three-step Winkler question, with part marks.
Reason needed in (a); quarter ratio in (b); 0.19 and fallback 0.32 in (c).
Mean marks about 0.57 per part; weaker candidates confused species; many gave mol dm−3.
Some used 2 instead of 4 for iodide moles.
A three-step reaction process proved hard for weaker SL candidates.

cards.difficulty_signal: Mean about 0.57/1 on each part of 24N.2.HL.TZ0.7; it discriminated well.

cards.title: Displacement results rank metals

walkthrough.question:
A student tests metals X, Y and Z in solutions of each other's ions.
X(s) with Z2+(aq): no reaction
Y(s) with X2+(aq): no reaction
Z(s) with Y2+(aq): reaction occurs
What is the order of the metals from least reactive to most reactive?
A. X, Y, Z
B. Y, X, Z
C. Z, X, Y
D. Y, Z, X
walkthrough.key_idea: A metal displaces only the ions of a less reactive metal.
walkthrough.careful: No reaction means the solid metal is the less reactive.
procedure: Write one inequality for each test.
Reaction: solid metal is more reactive than the ion's metal.
No reaction: solid metal is less reactive than the ion's metal.
Chain the inequalities into a single order.
Read whether the order wanted is increasing or decreasing.
tricks: Test each option against one no-reaction result; most options fail at once.
Increasing lists the least reactive first: reverse your chain if needed.
if_lost: What does a reaction tell you about the solid metal?
What does no reaction tell you about the two metals?
Can you write one inequality from each test?
Does the question want the weakest or strongest metal first?

1_context.short: Interpret supplied results, without recalling any reactivity series.
1_context.why: The syllabus says the relative reactivity need not be learned, so every question must supply data like this.
1_context.avoid: Trying to identify X, Y and Z as real metals.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.3: interpret data regarding metal and metal ion reactions.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books often show an activity series to memorise. Exams give unnamed metals, and no-reaction results carry as much information as reactions.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Each result gives a pair; only Y, X, Z fits all.
2_markscheme_logic.why: A valid order must satisfy all three tests at once, so one matching test is not enough.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Using only the single reaction and ignoring the no-reaction results.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: An order that fits only one test is wrong; every result must hold.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B fits all three tests. D fits the reaction test alone but puts X above Z.

3_novel_application.short: Letters replace metals, so memory cannot help.
3_novel_application.why: The logic is only comparison, so it transfers directly to a named metal such as thallium.
3_novel_application.disguise: Unnamed metals, or a heavy metal such as thallium that is rarely studied.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Solid metal against ion's metal: reaction means solid wins; no reaction means ion's metal wins.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: pick the one consistent order.
4_command_terms.why: Only one order satisfies every result, so the option check is decisive.
4_command_terms.avoid: Answering with the most reactive first.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the order from least to most reactive that fits all three results.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Write three inequalities, then chain them.
5_time_efficiency.why: Three short comparisons replace any drawn table and leave the order visible.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip writing ionic equations; only who beats whom matters.

6_data_booklet.short: Unknown metals: section 19 cannot help here.
6_data_booklet.why: X, Y and Z have no E° values, so the reasoning rests entirely on the given results.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up values for metals that are only letters.
6_data_booklet.pattern: No table applies to unnamed metals.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: reaction means the solid metal is more reactive than the ion's metal.

7_elimination.short: Each wrong order contradicts one test directly.
7_elimination.why: Each wrong order fails at a single result, so full ranking is not needed to reject it.

definitely_wrong.rule: It places Y above X, but Y did not displace X.
It makes Z least reactive, but Z displaced Y.
It makes X most reactive, but X did not displace Z.

walkthrough.answer: B. Test 1 gives Z > X, test 2 gives X > Y, test 3 gives Z > Y; so increasing order is Y, X, Z.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.3: interpret metal and metal ion reaction data; predict relative ease of oxidation.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books present series to recall; exams ask for an experimental design or a ranking from supplied results.

trigger_phrases: place the metal in a solution of the other metal's salt
if reaction occurs, the added metal is more reactive
more negative E°, more readily oxidized
trap_boundaries: In 25N.2.HL.6221.2(c) only one correct metal observation and explanation is capped at [1 max].
'No reaction' is accepted as an observation for the less reactive metal (25N.2.HL.6221.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Written design: full credit gives the test and what each outcome means; the test alone is partial (25M.2.HL.6215.2).

disguises: Unnamed metals in a results grid.
Designing a test for a rarely studied metal such as thallium.
Choosing metals that do or do not displace nickel from solution.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Name the solid and the ion; ask which metal would rather be the ion.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ all or nothing; written design items award one mark for the method and one for interpreting the outcome.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not set up a voltaic cell when a simple metal-in-solution test answers it (19M.2.HL.TZ2.4).

6_data_booklet.hack: For named metals in section 19, the more negative E° belongs to the metal more readily oxidized. Unnamed metals are not listed.

rules: Any order contradicting a single test result is wrong.
Check direction: increasing starts with the least reactive.

evidence.note: Worked question; answer B.
Two equivalent displacement tests, each with outcome interpretation.
Mn and Cu added to nickel solution; mark cap for one metal.
Many set up voltaic cells or failed to describe placing the metal in salt solutions.
Most could place metals in order from given data.

cards.difficulty_signal: The thallium and copper reactivity test was listed as difficult in May 2025 reports; no percentage is available for the worked MCQ.

cards.title: Label a voltaic cell from E° values

walkthrough.question:
A voltaic cell uses a Ni(s) electrode with Ni(NO3)2(aq) and a Ag(s) electrode with AgNO3(aq). The diagram shows two beakers joined through a voltmeter, with the left electrode marked anode and the right electrode marked cathode.
(a) State which electrode and electrolyte belong on each side, and show the direction of electron flow. Use section 19 of the data booklet. [2]
(b) Outline why a salt bridge must join the two half-cells. [1]
walkthrough.key_idea: More negative E° half-cell is the anode; electrons leave it through the wire.
walkthrough.question_type: Voltaic cell: label electrodes and electron flow
walkthrough.careful: Electrons travel through the external wire, never the salt bridge.
procedure: Look up both reduction potentials in section 19.
The metal with the more negative E° is oxidized: anode.
Pair each electrode with a solution of its own ions.
Draw electron flow along the wire from anode to cathode.
Salt bridge: ions move to keep each half-cell neutral.
tricks: Anode oxidation both begin with vowels; cathode reduction both begin with consonants.
Voltaic anode is negative; fails in electrolytic cells, where the anode is positive.
if_lost: Which metal has the more negative E° in section 19?
Does that metal lose or gain electrons?
At which electrode does oxidation take place?
What would build up in each beaker without a salt bridge?

1_context.short: Build the cell from data, then explain the bridge.
1_context.why: E° decides which half-cell is oxidized, and every label follows from that one decision.
1_context.avoid: Assuming the metal named first is the anode.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.6: explain electron flow from anode to cathode and ion movement across the salt bridge.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show a finished diagram, often Zn and Cu. Exams give a blank one and expect every label deduced from E°.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Electrode and electrolyte together for M1; wire arrow for M2.
2_markscheme_logic.why: M1 pairs metals with their own solutions on both sides; M2 needs an electron path through the external circuit.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Omitting the electron arrow: many missed this instruction (24N.2.HL.TZ0.8 report).
trigger_phrases: anode: Ni AND Ni(NO3)2 or Ni2+
cathode: Ag AND AgNO3 or Ag+
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The electron arrow must clearly run through the external circuit for M2.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Mean 1.4/2 in (a): correct electrodes alone earn one mark; the electron arrow earns the second.

3_novel_application.short: Blank labels and a pre-marked anode side test E° reading.
3_novel_application.why: Fixed anode and cathode labels mean you must place the right metal under each, not choose a side.
3_novel_application.avoid: Placing the metals first and changing the printed labels.
3_novel_application.disguise: Pre-marked anode and cathode positions with no metals shown look like a recall drawing.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Read the side's label, then ask which metal must be oxidized or reduced there.

4_command_terms.short: Label needs symbols; outline needs one brief reason.
4_command_terms.why: Outline requires only a short account, and either accepted idea earns the single mark.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing a paragraph on the salt bridge for one mark.
4_command_terms.demands: Mark electrodes, electrolytes and electron direction, then give one purpose of the bridge.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: (a) two separate marks: placement, then electron flow. (b) one mark for one accepted reason.

5_time_efficiency.short: Compare two values, label, arrow, one line on bridge.
5_time_efficiency.why: One comparison fixes all labels, and the salt bridge line can be learned.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating E°cell: it is not asked for.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip half-equations and E°cell; neither is requested.

6_data_booklet.why: The table ranks oxidation tendency, so reading two values replaces memorising any metal series.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Citing old section numbers printed on legacy papers: section 19 holds potentials in the current booklet.
6_data_booklet.pattern: The half-cell listed higher, with more negative E°, is the anode.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: anode is oxidation, electrons go through the wire, and the salt bridge carries ions.

7_elimination.short: Electrons never enter the salt bridge or solution.
7_elimination.why: Electrons move only in metal conductors; solutions and the bridge conduct by moving ions.
7_elimination.avoid: Saying that the salt bridge carries electrons (03M.2.HL.TZ0.7 report).

definitely_wrong.target: Electron arrows through the salt bridge or solutions
definitely_wrong.rule: Electrons travel only through the external wire.
Ag has the more positive E°, so its ion is reduced.

definitely_wrong.target: Bridge purpose given as carrying electrons
definitely_wrong.rule: The bridge moves ions only.

walkthrough.answer: (a) Anode: Ni in Ni(NO3)2/Ni2+; cathode: Ag in AgNO3/Ag+ [1]. Electrons flow anode to cathode through the wire, left to right [1]. (b) It balances charges and keeps each half-cell neutral, or completes the circuit by allowing ion flow [1].

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.5 and R3.2.6: identify electrodes and explain electron and ion flow in a primary cell.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show a complete Zn/Cu picture; exams ask for missing components, labels and arrows on a partial sketch.

trigger_phrases: salt bridge immersed in both half-cells
trap_boundaries: Salt bridge must touch the solutions for its mark (25N.2.HL.6209.5).
Wires must be connected for the voltmeter mark (25N.2.HL.6209.5).
Components may be scored from a clear diagram (25N.1B.HL.6220.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit needs bridge in contact, connected voltmeter, ions and correctly labelled electrodes; a drawing with a floating bridge loses a mark.

disguises: Complete a partly drawn Mn/Ni cell.
Label a pre-marked anode and cathode.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Every voltaic drawing needs the same checklist: two own-ion beakers, wire, voltmeter, bridge in solution.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Separate marks for placement, electron flow and the bridge reason; drawing items mark each component.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not add half-equations or E°cell unless asked.

6_data_booklet.hack: Use section 19 to pick the anode: the more negative E° half-cell. Cell labels themselves are NOT in the booklet.

rules: Electrons never pass through the salt bridge or solution.
Never put a metal in another metal's ion solution for a standard half-cell.
Signs flip between voltaic and electrolytic; oxidation at the anode does not.

evidence.note: Label electrodes, electrolytes and electron flow; salt bridge reason.
Mark split, and electron path through the external circuit.
Mean 1.4/2 and 0.83/1; electron flow often missing.
Salt bridge contact and connected wires are conditions for marks.
Salt bridge and voltmeter may score from a clear diagram.
A minority thought the salt bridge allowed electrons to flow.
Bridge missing, unlabelled or not touching solutions; electron direction wrong.
Electrons drawn through the salt bridge rather than the wire.

cards.difficulty_signal: Mean 1.4/2 on labelling in 24N.2.HL.TZ0.8; 'salt bridge' and 'voltaic cell' are frequent error signals, and drawing a voltaic cell was flagged as difficult in May 2011.

cards.title: What changes while a voltaic cell runs

walkthrough.question:
Two half-cells, metal Z in Z2+(aq) and metal X in X2+(aq), are joined by a voltmeter and a salt bridge.
X2+(aq) + 2e− ⇌ X(s) E° = +0.25 V
Z2+(aq) + 2e− ⇌ Z(s) E° = −0.60 V
Which change happens while this cell produces electricity?
A. Positive ions in the salt bridge move to the Z half-cell.
B. Electrons move from the X half-cell to the Z half-cell.
C. The X2+ concentration rises.
D. The Z electrode loses mass.
walkthrough.key_idea: Anode metal dissolves; electrons and cations both head towards the cathode half-cell.
walkthrough.question_type: Voltaic cell: predict changes during operation
walkthrough.careful: Cations in the bridge move towards the cathode half-cell.
procedure: Compare E° values; the more negative metal is the anode.
Write oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode.
Electrons move along the wire from anode to cathode.
In the bridge, cations go to cathode, anions to anode.
Anode metal loses mass; its ion concentration rises.
Cathode metal gains mass; its ion concentration falls.
tricks: Only the anode's metal can dissolve; fails for an inert electrode half-cell.
Cations follow electrons towards the cathode half-cell.
if_lost: Which half-cell has the more negative E°?
Is that half-cell's metal oxidized or reduced?
In which direction do electrons move along the wire?
Which ions must arrive to balance charge at each half-cell?

1_context.short: One E° comparison predicts every change in the cell.
1_context.why: Once the anode is known, electron flow, ion flow, mass changes and concentrations all follow.
1_context.avoid: Treating each option as a separate fact to recall.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.6: explain electron flow from anode to cathode and ion movement across the salt bridge.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books label one static diagram. This question asks what changes over time, including concentrations and electrode mass.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only electrode Z losing mass matches anode oxidation.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Oxidation turns solid Z into Z2+ ions in solution, so the electrode gets lighter.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Having the wrong electrode losing mass, reported in 18M.2.HL.TZ1.6.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The other three options each reverse one direction: ions, electrons or concentration.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D follows from Z being the anode. A, B and C are what you would pick if X were the anode.

3_novel_application.short: Letters X and Z hide which metal is the anode.
3_novel_application.why: Only the E° values identify the anode, so name recognition does not help.
3_novel_application.avoid: Assuming the electrode drawn on the left is the anode.
3_novel_application.disguise: Unnamed metals, and options describing different particles and quantities.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Write Z → Z2+ + 2e− on the page, and test each option against this one line.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: test each statement against the anode.
4_command_terms.why: Each statement is independently true or false, so one correct check is enough.
4_command_terms.avoid: Stopping to explain why the others fail once D is proved.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the single true statement about a working cell.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Find the anode, write its equation, test options.
5_time_efficiency.why: Everything reduces to one comparison and one equation, so this item should be quick.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating E°cell: the size of the voltage is irrelevant here.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the E°cell value; only the sign order of the two values matters.

6_data_booklet.short: Values are given; X and Z are not in section 19.
6_data_booklet.why: The question provides the two potentials, so no lookup is needed.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for metals X and Z in the table.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Use the two given values: more negative is the anode.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: anode is oxidation, and cations in the bridge go to the cathode.

7_elimination.short: Once Z is the anode, A, B and C reverse directions.
7_elimination.why: Each wrong option needs X to be the anode, which contradicts the E° values.
7_elimination.avoid: Thinking positive ions go to the anode half-cell because it builds positive charge is wrong only in reverse: check.

definitely_wrong.rule: Cations move to the cathode half-cell, and Z is the anode.
Electrons leave the anode, which is Z.
X2+ is reduced at the cathode, so it is used up.

walkthrough.answer: D. Z has the more negative E°, so it is oxidized at the anode and dissolves, losing mass.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.5, R3.2.6: identify electrode signs and explain electron and ion movement.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books describe a cell at one moment; exams ask how mass, concentration and ions change as it runs, and about electrode signs.

Silver cathode is positive in a voltaic cell; many picked the wrong sign and name (25M.1A.SL.TZ2.28).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial knowledge names the electrodes; full credit gives separate directions for each ion type and the mass changes.

disguises: Unnamed metals in a cell.
Statements about mass or concentration instead of electrode names.
Zinc as both negative electrode and reducing agent.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not calculate E°cell when the question only asks what changes.

6_data_booklet.hack: For named metals, section 19 gives the anode: more negative E°. Ion directions are NOT in the booklet.

rules: Any option treating the more positive E° metal as dissolving is wrong for a metal/ion cell.
Electrons flow from the more negative half-cell in a voltaic cell.

cards.title: E°cell: right size, right sign

walkthrough.question:
A voltaic cell joins a Ag(s)/Ag+(aq) half-cell to a Mg(s)/Mg2+(aq) half-cell with a salt bridge and voltmeter.
Ag+(aq) + e− ⇌ Ag(s) E° = +0.80 V
Mg2+(aq) + 2e− ⇌ Mg(s) E° = −2.37 V
What is E°cell?
A. −3.17 V
B. −1.57 V
C. +1.57 V
D. +3.17 V
walkthrough.key_idea: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and a working cell's value is positive.
walkthrough.question_type: Standard cell potential from E° values
walkthrough.careful: Never scale E° by coefficients; keep the positive sign.
procedure: Find both reduction potentials in the question or section 19.
More positive E° half-cell is the cathode; the other is the anode.
Calculate E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.
Leave E° values unchanged, whatever the electron coefficients.
Write the answer with its positive sign and unit.
tricks: Opposite signs: add the magnitudes. Same signs: subtract them.
A working voltaic cell always gives a positive answer.
if_lost: Which half-cell has the more positive E°?
Which half-cell undergoes reduction in a working cell?
What sign must E°cell have for a spontaneous reaction?

1_context.short: E°cell from two reduction potentials; sign shows spontaneity.
1_context.why: A voltaic cell runs by a spontaneous reaction, and that is what a positive E°cell means.
1_context.avoid: Treating the sign as a matter of order of subtraction.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.13: E°cell is calculated from standard electrode potentials and is positive for a spontaneous reaction.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books drill the subtraction. This exam tests the meaning: both signs of the same size appear as options.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only +3.17 V scores; −3.17 V earns nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Same magnitude with a wrong sign shows no grasp that a voltaic cell is spontaneous, and MCQs have no partial credit.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Choosing −3.17 V: 19% got the value with the wrong sign (25M.1A.HL.6213.37 report).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: A correct magnitude is not enough: sign is part of the answer.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D keeps the positive sign; A is the same arithmetic with the sign reversed.

3_novel_application.short: Different electron numbers tempt you into scaling.
3_novel_application.why: E° is intensive: it describes a potential per electron, so it does not change with the coefficient in an equation.
3_novel_application.avoid: Doubling 0.80 because Mg transfers two electrons.
3_novel_application.disguise: Coefficients of 1e− and 2e− suggest that the silver value should be doubled.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Coefficient scaling belongs to equations and ΔG°, never to E° values.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: select the value with correct sign.
4_command_terms.why: All options use the same two numbers, so the choice tests your method and sign.
4_command_terms.avoid: Picking the first option showing the right digits.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the correct value of E°cell, including its sign.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Larger minus smaller; values straddle zero, so add.
5_time_efficiency.why: Values on either side of zero always give a gap equal to the sum of their sizes.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing out the full cell equation.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the balanced overall equation; E°cell needs only two numbers.

6_data_booklet.short: Values given here; section 19 lists them otherwise.
6_data_booklet.why: Written questions direct you to section 19, and a misread line gives a wrong value.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Reading the wrong line, reported for copper in 03M.2.HL.TZ0.7.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 19 lists reductions from most negative to most positive; the lower one is the cathode.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and that positive means spontaneous.

7_elimination.short: Negative options fail; gap must exceed 2.37.
7_elimination.why: A voltaic cell's reaction is spontaneous, so negative options go. Values on either side of zero must differ by more than either value alone.
7_elimination.avoid: Adding signed values, 0.80 + (−2.37), which gives the 1.57 distractors.

definitely_wrong.rule: A negative value contradicts a working voltaic cell.
A negative value contradicts a working voltaic cell.
Values straddling zero must differ by more than 2.37 V.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.13: calculate E°cell from electrode potentials; positive for a spontaneous reaction.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stop at subtraction; exams offer both signs, and examiners read a wrong sign as weak understanding of spontaneity.

trigger_phrases: E°cell calculated from two section 19 values
trap_boundaries: Wrong sign scores nothing in MCQs (25M.1A.HL.6213.37).
Wrong line from the booklet gives wrong answers, such as +1.02 V (13M.2.HL.TZ1.4).
Written form: 0.92 V for Mn/Ni scores [1] (25N.2.HL.6209.5).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Same digits, opposite sign: the mark turns on knowing that a working cell has a positive value.

disguises: Half-equations with unequal electrons.
Both E° values negative, as for Al and Ni.
Mixed in with a cell drawing.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ignore coefficients. Picture a number line: E°cell is always the distance from anode up to cathode.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ all or nothing. Written items often award [1] for the value alone, shown with sign and unit.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not write half-equations or scale them.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 19 is ordered from most negative to most positive; lower value in the table is the cathode. The subtraction rule is NOT in the booklet.

rules: Negative E°cell cannot be a working voltaic cell.
If values straddle zero, E°cell is larger than either magnitude.
Same-sign values give a difference smaller than the larger magnitude.

evidence.note: Worked question; answer D.
59% scored; 19% obtained the value with the wrong sign, showing weak grasp of spontaneity.
Same type with Al and Ni; answer C.
Written form, Mn/Ni: 0.92 V for one mark.
Wrong sign used or wrong data chosen in E° calculation.
Generally done well, though some found negative answers.
Wrong manganese potential, and many gave +1.02 V.
Wrong copper value carelessly quoted from the booklet.

cards.difficulty_signal: The pack's statistics list 19% correct, but the report says 59% scored and 19% had the right value with the wrong sign. Standard cell potential was flagged as difficult in May 2025.

cards.title: Use E° to predict spontaneity

walkthrough.question:
Three standard electrode potentials are given:
Zn2+(aq) + 2e− ⇌ Zn(s) E° = −0.76 V
Fe2+(aq) + 2e− ⇌ Fe(s) E° = −0.45 V
Ni2+(aq) + 2e− ⇌ Ni(s) E° = −0.26 V
Which pair reacts spontaneously under standard conditions?
A. Zn and Fe2+
B. Fe and Zn2+
C. Ni and Zn2+
D. Ni and Fe2+
walkthrough.key_idea: A metal reduces ions whose half-cell has a more positive E°.
walkthrough.careful: The ion's half-cell is cathode; the metal's half-cell is anode.
procedure: For each option, treat the ion as the species reduced.
Treat the metal as the species oxidized.
Calculate E°cell = E°(ion's half-cell) − E°(metal's half-cell).
A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous.
Choose the pair, or justify the outcome, using that sign.
tricks: The reacting metal lies above the ion's line; fails if the table is reversed.
Most negative E° metal is the strongest reducing agent listed.
if_lost: In each option, which species would lose electrons?
Which metal listed is most easily oxidized?
What sign of E°cell shows a spontaneous reaction?

1_context.short: Sign of E°cell, not table memory, predicts the reaction.
1_context.why: Writing reduction and oxidation roles for each pair turns the table into a direct prediction.
1_context.avoid: Answering from recall of reactivity without using the given values.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.13: predict whether a reaction is spontaneous in the forward or reverse direction from E° data.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach the calculation for cells. Exams hide it inside pairs of species with no cell drawn.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only Zn with Fe2+ gives a positive E°cell.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Zn's half-cell is more negative, so Zn can give electrons to Fe2+; all other pairs have the less reactive metal.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Picking a pair by metal and ion being close together in the list.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: In written answers, position in the table alone is not enough (04M.2.HL.TZ0.10): give E° values or their sign.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A has a metal more reactive than the ion's metal. B, C and D have it the other way round.

3_novel_application.short: No cell is drawn, yet it is a cell question.
3_novel_application.why: Any metal and ion pair is a hidden cell: the same subtraction works without any apparatus.
3_novel_application.avoid: Thinking cell potential applies only when a cell is shown.
3_novel_application.disguise: A question about species reacting with no mention of a cell or E°cell.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Metal and ion in one line? Ion's half-cell minus metal's half-cell, and read the sign.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: find the one feasible pair.
4_command_terms.why: Three pairs have the wrong order, so only one can give a positive value.
4_command_terms.avoid: Ticking two pairs: there is one correct row.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the single pair that gives a positive E°cell.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Check metal is more negative than ion. Done.
5_time_efficiency.why: Only the order of two values matters, so no subtraction is really required.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating E°cell for all four options.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the exact E°cell values and overall equations.

6_data_booklet.short: All needed values appear here; section 19 otherwise.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 19 lists E° values, so the comparison never depends on memorised reactivity.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Reading a half-equation backwards and flipping the sign of its value.
6_data_booklet.pattern: In section 19, a metal reduces ions listed in lines below it.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: positive E°cell means spontaneous.

7_elimination.short: Reject pairs where the metal is less negative.
7_elimination.why: A metal with a less negative E° cannot give electrons to an ion of a more easily oxidized metal.
7_elimination.avoid: Thinking Ni is most reactive because −0.26 looks largest or least negative in size.

definitely_wrong.rule: Fe's E° is less negative than Zn's, so Fe cannot reduce Zn2+.
Ni's E° is less negative than Zn's, so Ni cannot reduce Zn2+.
Ni's E° is less negative than Fe's, so Ni cannot reduce Fe2+.

walkthrough.answer: A. Zn and Fe2+: E°cell = −0.45 − (−0.76) = +0.31 V, which is positive.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.12, R3.2.13: interpret E° data; predict spontaneity in either direction.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach E°cell for drawn cells; exams use it to judge displacement, observations or stronger reducing agents.

trap_boundaries: Saying one ion is above another is not enough; give E° values or a sign (04M.2.HL.TZ0.10).
In 25N.2.HL.6221.2(c), an explanation for only one metal is capped at [1 max].
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: right prediction. Full: right prediction plus comparison of E° values or reducing strength.

disguises: Species pairs with no cell drawn.
Choosing metals that coat with nickel.
Zinc protecting iron.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Any metal plus an ion is a possible cell; read the sign.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ all or nothing; written items award prediction and justification separately.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not compute all four potentials; compare the order of two values.

6_data_booklet.hack: Read section 19 as a ladder: each metal can reduce ions lower down. Spontaneity rule is NOT in the booklet.

rules: Metal with a less negative E° than the ion's line cannot react under standard conditions.
Check standard conditions: non-standard concentration can shift this outcome.

evidence.note: Worked question; answer A.
About 50% could use the data to predict the displacement.
Accepted comparisons: E°, readily oxidized, or reducing agent strength.
'Above' or 'below' alone not sufficient; work out E° values.
Some missed that zinc is a stronger reducing agent than iron.
Predictions were often correct but not properly justified.

cards.difficulty_signal: About 50% on the worked item; 'standard electrode' and 'electrode potential' are frequent error signals, and manipulation of potentials was flagged in May 2017.

cards.title: The hydrogen electrode's zero is assigned

walkthrough.question:
Which statement about the E° value of the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is correct?
A. It was found by experiment.
B. It changes with temperature.
C. It was assigned by choice.
D. It changes with the other electrode used.
walkthrough.key_idea: The SHE's zero is a chosen reference, not a measured value.
walkthrough.careful: Zero is assigned, so no measurement or condition can change it.
procedure: Recall that the SHE's E° is defined as 0 V.
Decide whether each statement treats zero as chosen or measured.
Reject statements that make E° depend on conditions.
Separate the SHE's E° from a measured cell potential.
tricks: Anything making the SHE's zero depend on something is false.
Fails for cell potential: it does depend on H2 pressure and acid.
if_lost: Can a single electrode's potential be measured without a second electrode?
Why would tables of E° values need one reference half-cell?
What would measuring against a reference tell you?

1_context.short: Tests what the zero means, not just its value.
1_context.why: Only potential differences can be measured, so one half-cell was given a value and all others compared with it.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.12: the hydrogen half-cell has a potential of zero by convention.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show a labelled SHE and move on. Exams ask about how the value arises and what it does not depend on.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Arbitrarily set is correct; 'measured' is the common error.
2_markscheme_logic.why: A value set by agreement cannot be experimental or depend on conditions, so the alternatives all fail together.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Choosing 'experimentally determined', the common wrong answer (24N.1.HL.TZ0.31 report).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The zero is fixed, yet a cell using the SHE can still respond to H2 pressure or acid choice (25N.1A.HL.6219.36).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: C treats 0 V as a convention. A treats it as a measured result.

3_novel_application.short: Reasonable-sounding statements hide a definition question.
3_novel_application.why: Other electrode potentials really are experimental, which makes statement A sound natural for the SHE too.
3_novel_application.avoid: Extending facts about other half-cells to the reference.
3_novel_application.disguise: Options sound like general lab facts about electrodes.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: is this about the reference itself or about what is measured against it?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: find one true statement.
4_command_terms.why: Only one statement fits a defined value; the others treat it as a physical measurement.
4_command_terms.avoid: Overthinking wording about temperature in other half-cells.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the one correct statement about the SHE's E° value.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Recall 'by convention'; pick the matching option.
5_time_efficiency.why: This is a recall of one idea, so spare the time for calculation items.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Working through each statement in depth.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip thinking about the SHE apparatus; this item does not test it.

6_data_booklet.why: The table shows the value and its central place, but not why it was given that value.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Reading 0.00 V as a measured value because it is in a data table.
6_data_booklet.pattern: H+ + e− ⇌ ½H2 at 0.00 V splits negative and positive values.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: the zero is assigned by convention, and the SHE's set-up and conditions.

7_elimination.short: A defined zero cannot vary or be measured.
7_elimination.why: Definitions are fixed by agreement, so statements describing dependence or measurement cannot apply to it.
7_elimination.avoid: Thinking D is true because E°cell changes with the other electrode: that is the cell value, not the SHE's.

definitely_wrong.rule: An assigned reference is not an experimental result.
A defined value does not vary with temperature.
A reference cannot depend on what is measured against it.

walkthrough.answer: C. The 0 V is assigned by convention as the reference for all other half-cells.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.12: hydrogen half-cell potential is zero by convention and is used to measure E°.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show the apparatus; exams test what the zero means and which conditions matter to measured cell potentials.

trap_boundaries: SHE need not be the anode, and acid choice and H2 pressure still matter to the cell (25N.1A.HL.6219.36).
Carbon is ruled out as the SHE electrode; platinum is typical (11M.1.HL.TZ1.32).
Definitions of standard electrode potential need standard conditions and the SHE (12M.2.HL.TZ1.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Knowing the value scores nothing here; the mark depends on how the value arises.

disguises: Statements about temperature, pressure or acid identity.
Whether the SHE must be the anode.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Separate the assigned E° of the SHE from the measured potential of the cell that contains it.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ all or nothing; written definitions reward standard conditions and reference to the SHE.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not rebuild the SHE drawing for a statement question.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 19 shows 0.00 V for H+/H2, but why and the set-up are NOT in the booklet.

rules: Reject any claim that the SHE's zero was measured.
Reject any claim that the SHE's E° changes with conditions; measured cell potentials can change.

evidence.note: Worked question; answer C.
About 40% correct; many thought the value was found experimentally.
SHE statements; answer B, 0 V at any temperature.
Carbon electrode ruled out for the SHE; platinum is typical; 79.75% correct.
Definitions omitted standard conditions or SHE reference.
Structure and conditions of the SHE gave varied marks; some drew two half-cells.

cards.difficulty_signal: About 40% correct on the worked item, one of the pack's five hardest; the SHE was flagged as difficult in November 2024 and May 2019.

cards.title: ΔG° and E°cell have opposite signs

walkthrough.question:
A voltaic cell reaction has positive ΔH° and positive ΔS°. Using ΔG° = −nFE°, which statement is correct?
A. E°cell rises when temperature rises.
B. E°cell falls when temperature rises.
C. E°cell stays the same when temperature rises.
D. ΔG° is above zero at every temperature.
walkthrough.key_idea: Heating lowers ΔG° when ΔS° is positive, so E° goes up.
walkthrough.careful: ΔG° and E° always have opposite signs.
procedure: Write ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and ΔG° = −nFE°.
Decide how ΔG° changes with the given variable.
Convert with opposite sign: ΔG° down means E° up.
For numbers, use J, correct n and F from section 2.
tricks: Positive ΔS°: raising T makes ΔG° more negative. Assumes ΔH° and ΔS° stay constant.
In calculations, check n from the half-equation before substituting.
if_lost: Which term in ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° contains temperature?
With positive ΔS°, how does that term change on heating?
How does E° relate in sign to ΔG°?

1_context.short: Joins two booklet equations through ΔG°.
1_context.why: ΔG° appears in both equations, so a change in temperature passes from one equation to the other.
1_context.avoid: Thinking of temperature as affecting E° only through collisions or rates.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.14: ΔG° = −nFE°cell relates Gibbs energy change and standard cell potential.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use the equation for a single calculation. Here it must be combined with ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° qualitatively.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Rising T lowers ΔG°, raising E°cell: statement A.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The term −TΔS° becomes more negative as T rises, and the minus sign in −nFE° then raises E°.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Choosing B by forgetting the minus sign in −nFE°.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The sign link matters: a falling ΔG° with a falling E° loses the mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A uses both equations; B uses the first and misses the sign in the second.

3_novel_application.short: No numbers: pure sign reasoning from two equations.
3_novel_application.why: With no numbers, the only route is tracking the direction of each term.
3_novel_application.avoid: Looking for numerical data to substitute.
3_novel_application.disguise: A thermodynamics equation inside an electrochemistry item, with no values.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Mark each term with an up or down arrow as T rises, then pass arrows along.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: choose the correct trend statement.
4_command_terms.why: Options exhaust the three possible trends, plus a claim about ΔG°.
4_command_terms.avoid: Reading D as a safe-sounding general statement.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the statement fitting how E°cell responds to temperature.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: T up, ΔG° down, E° up: three arrows.
5_time_efficiency.why: Three arrows replace any algebra, and the same method covers a negative ΔS°.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Rearranging into an algebraic expression for E°.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip symbolic rearrangement; arrows suffice.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 1 has both equations; section 2 has F.
6_data_booklet.why: Both relations can be read directly, so no recall is required, only sign logic.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Memorising the equations when they are printed.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 1: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and ΔG° = −nFE°. Section 2: F = 9.65 × 10^4 C mol−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: the sign link to spontaneity and how to find n.

7_elimination.short: T appears in ΔG°, and voltaic means spontaneous.
7_elimination.why: Non-zero ΔS° makes ΔG° temperature dependent. A voltaic cell also needs negative ΔG° at the conditions it runs.
7_elimination.avoid: Assuming that a standard value cannot depend on temperature.

definitely_wrong.rule: With non-zero ΔS°, ΔG° changes with T, so E° must too.
A voltaic reaction is spontaneous, and positive ΔS° makes ΔG° more negative on heating.
Falling E° needs rising ΔG°, but positive ΔS° lowers it.

cards.title: Secondary cells: half-equation and comment on E°

walkthrough.question:

walkthrough.key_idea: Discharge anode is Li losing an electron; large negative E° means easy oxidation.
walkthrough.question_type: Secondary cell: half-equation and E° comment
walkthrough.careful: Interpret −3.04 V; quoting it alone earns no mark.
procedure: Note the electrode asked for and charging or discharging.
Discharge anode is oxidation: electrons on the product side.
Balance atoms and charge, including the electron.
Find the E° value in section 19.
Comment on both sign and size.
Link them to the direction of reaction.

On which side of the equation do electrons go for that process?
Where does lithium sit in section 19 compared with other metals?

1_context.avoid: Getting caught up in how the graphite layers work.

2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Only quoting −3.04 V, which many did and which was not enough (25M.2.HL.6221.6 report).

A value alone gives no comment.

cards.title: Name the mobile charge carrier

walkthrough.question: Solid potassium, K(s), and solid potassium chloride, KCl(s), both have lattice structures. Predict how well each conducts electricity and give a reason for each. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Conduction needs mobile charge: electrons in metals, ions in melts and solutions.
walkthrough.question_type: Conduction: identify the mobile charge carrier
walkthrough.careful: Explain KCl(s) with fixed ions, never with missing electrons.
procedure: Classify each substance as metal or ionic.
State the conductivity level for each substance.
Name the charge carrier for that type.
Say whether that carrier can move in this state.
tricks: Solid ionic: ions fixed. Melt or solution: ions move. Metal wire: electrons move.

if_lost: What type of bonding holds K(s) together?
What charged particles does KCl contain?
Can those particles change position in a solid lattice?

1_context.short: Basis for electrolysis: what actually carries the current.

1_context.avoid: Thinking that any charged particle automatically conducts.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.8: explain how current is conducted in an electrolytic cell.

trigger_phrases: high conductivity AND delocalized electrons free to move
low conductivity AND ions fixed in position

4_command_terms.demands: Give each substance's expected conductivity and the particle-level reason.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per substance, for prediction and reason together. [1 max] for predictions alone.

5_time_efficiency.short: One line for K(s), one line for KCl(s).
5_time_efficiency.why: Two short sentences cover both marks, with the keywords doing the work.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Explaining the molten case when only solids are asked for.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip conductivity in melts or solutions; the question asks only about solids.

6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for conductivity values in a booklet section.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: metals conduct by delocalized electrons, and ionic compounds conduct only when ions can move.

7_elimination.short: Electron-based reasons for KCl(s) are always wrong.
7_elimination.why: Current in an ionic substance is carried by ions, so lack of electrons is not the explanation.
7_elimination.avoid: Writing that molten ionic compounds conduct via electrons (04M.2.SL.TZ0.6).

definitely_wrong.target: KCl(s) does not conduct because it has no free electrons
definitely_wrong.rule: The markscheme rejects electron explanations here.

definitely_wrong.target: KCl(s) conducts because it contains ions

definitely_wrong.target: K(s) conducts because it is a metal
definitely_wrong.rule: The moving electrons must be stated.

trap_boundaries: [1 max] for predictions with no reasons (24N.2.HL.TZ0.3).

2_markscheme_logic.delta: A bare prediction earns little. Naming the particle and whether it can move earns the mark.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not add lattice energy or structure details.

rules: Any electron-based reason for current in an ionic liquid or solution is wrong.

5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing balanced half-equations for a one-mark MCQ.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip half-equations and E°; no competition exists in a melt.

6_data_booklet.pattern: No table is needed for a melt.

7_elimination.avoid: Picking ozone: few did (25M.1A.HL.6219.37 report), but it stays wrong.

definitely_wrong.rule: Al cannot form at the anode, where oxidation occurs.
Al cannot form at the anode, where oxidation occurs.

cards.title: Aqueous electrolysis: water competes

walkthrough.question: Dilute KCl(aq) is electrolysed using inert electrodes, as one of two cells connected in series. State the half-equation at the anode (positive electrode) and at the cathode (negative electrode). Use section 19 of the data booklet. [2]

walkthrough.careful: Dilute chloride gives oxygen, not chlorine; K+ is not reduced.
procedure: List the solution's ions plus water for each electrode.
Cathode: the species with the most positive E° is reduced.
Anode: the species with the least positive E° is oxidized.

Write each half-equation with electrons on the correct side.
tricks: Group 1 and 2 ions stay in solution: the cathode gives hydrogen.
Dilute halide gives O2; concentrated chloride gives Cl2. Applies to halides only.

Which has the more positive E°: K+ or water?
Is the chloride here dilute or concentrated?
Which process happens at the anode?

1_context.avoid: Answering as if the solution were molten KCl.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.2.15: deduce products of aqueous electrolysis from standard electrode potentials.
